newsitem.title: NORWAY: Group of 48 banks to work to reduce forex risk.
newsitem.headline: Group of 48 banks to work to reduce forex risk.

text.p: A group of 48 major commercial and investment banks from about 20 countries said on Wednesday it established cooperation on a global system that will reduce foreign exchange settlement risk.
World foreign exchange turnover has soared 50 percent in the last three years to $1.2 trillion a day. But although trading volume has ballooned, the settlement process has not changed substantially.
The banks, known as the Group of 40 Banks (G40) for their original membership number, favour one industry solution for a new world settlement system with fair and open access.
It would strive to ensure optimised, effective risk-reduction through maximised geographical and currency coverage, according to a G40 statement released in Oslo.

Finn Otto Hansen, chairman of the G40 steering committee and a risk-management strategist at Norway's top commercial bank Den norske Bank (DnB), said 43 financial institutions participated in a meeting in London on Monday.
"We are glad to announce that also leading investment banks have accepted our invitation to participate in the group," he said.
Hansen said Goldman Sachs and Lehman Brothers were among the investment banks in the group.
"A few more are in the pipeline although they have not confirmed yet," he told Reuters. "We now have commercial and investment banks but we would not exclude savings banks."

It was the second session held by the group, which was formed in Florence, Italy, in October and includes leading banks from Australia, Britain, Germany, France, Italy, the United States and other countries.
"At the meeting, both representatives from the central banks (G10) and a third group (the G20) gave presentations of their work related to fx settlement issues," the statement said.

Bankers specialising in large value cross-border payments formed the G20 in 1994. It aims to set up a foreign exchange clearing system, based on the principle of Continuous Linked Settlements (CLS) that bridges and connects national payment systems.
"We are not planning to run the new system, but we are an interest group," Hansen said, describing the role of the G40.
"We have no intention of making our own systems, but we have comments of what the system should be, who should participate and later, the governance of such an organisation."
The statement said the following should form the basis for further development of admission criteria to a new system:

--To be included in the system, any country should have a strong investment grade rating of at least BBB+, a fully convertible currency and fully apply to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) guidelines with respect to capital adequacy requirements in relation to assets and derivatives.

--To be a member of the system, any bank should have a strong investment grade rating of at least BBB+, have a tier 1 capital of at least $1 billion and be a supervised institution fully compliant with BIS guidelines.

--Any bank who is a member should be of the top 200 participants in the fx market or be a fully fledged settler in the real-time gross settlement system of a currency included in the new world settlement system.
